title: Periodic Function
body:
$f$ is periodic with period $P$ when $f(x + P) = f(x)$ for all $x$. The **fundamental period** is
the smallest such $P > 0$; $\sin(nx)$ has fundamental period $2\pi/n$, so every term of a
[[Fourier Series]] repeats a whole number of times inside one period of the series itself. That is
the reason the expansion closes: the basis functions all share the interval.

A function need not be continuous to be expanded. **Piecewise continuous is enough**: finitely many
jumps in a period, each with finite one-sided limits. At a jump the series converges to the
*midpoint* of the two one-sided values rather than to either of them, and it overshoots on the way,
which is [[Gibbs Phenomenon]].

Any function on a bounded interval $[0, L]$ can be *treated* as periodic by repeating it, which is
how a [[Fourier Series]] applies to something defined only on a finite domain. That is the case
[[Partial Differential Equations]] actually uses.

Not to be confused with [[Continuity]] in [[CALCULUS 1]] or with the signal sense of
[[Continuous]] in [[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]].
